newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Oil, gasoline up on tight supplies, corn rises. [Corrected 21:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil, gasoline up on tight supplies, corn rises. [Corrected 21:55 GMT]

text.p: Gasoline led oil prices higher on Wednesday after weekly reports on petroleum stocks indicated a sharp drop in supplies.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline for August delivery closed 3.43 cents a gallon higher at 69.90 cents after setting a life-of-contract high during the session.

Buying was sparked by reports from the American Petroleum Institute late on Tuesday and the Department of Energy on Wednesday that said U.S. gasoline stockpiles had fallen from 3.1 million to 3.8 million barrels in the week ended July 25.
The agencies also said crude oil stocks had fallen from 9.7 million to 9.9 million barrels in the week.
September (corrects from August) crude oil jumped 45 cents to close at $20.30 a barrel and September (corrects from August) heating oil followed the other markets.

"There is basically a tightness in the cash market here and in the (U.S.) Gulf when there is steady high demand, so that has created tremendous pent up buying," said Michael Busby, trader at Northville Industries in Melville, N.Y.

Some analysts, pointing to a steady level of crude imports and a slight decline in U.S. refinery use, said the apparent big drop in crude stocks may have been due to the short-term effect of Hurricane Danny last week or a statistical quirk.
But local New York market factors kept gasoline buoyant and at the lead in the oil complex.

Oil industry sources said refiner Tosco Corp. shut down the big catalytic cracking unit at its Bayway refinery in New Jersey on Wednesday after detecting a catalyst leak. The facility usually produces 130,000 barrels of gasoline a day.
That tightness pushed demand for physical gasoline in the New York area market several cents above futures on Wednesday.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn prices closed higher on concerns about dry weather in parts of the Midwest and in the North China Plain, another key grain growing region.
Corn for September delivery rose 4-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $2.62-1/4.
"We're still dealing with weather that doesn't have a lot of water in it," said Dave Armstrong, grains analyst for ABN Amro/The Chicago Corp.

Gains were trimmed late on selling in the nearby soybean pit, as farmer sales of remaining on-farm supplies continued and country elevators and processors dropped back on cash bids for beans as they acquired supplies.
Soybeans for August delivery fell 10-1/2 cents a bushel to close at $7.56-1/2.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly trading was volatile ahead of first notice day for deliveries against the August futures next Monday.
August pork bellies closed down 0.75 cent a pound at 83.200 cents but February bellies closed up the 3.00 cent a pound daily trading limit at 75.150 cents.
"There's obviously a lot of rolling today because you have first notice day coming up Monday," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
He said the incentive to sell August came on concern that part of the deliverable supply was of low-grade bellies that are more suitable for the trimmings market.
